| [NOTE-811](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-811.md) | Kunz & Rittel — Issues as Elements of Information Systems | A short design statement, not a study. IBIS treats planning as an argumentative process whose atoms are issues, questions put because positions differ; arguments for and against positions run until an issue is settled, and a challenge to a supporting statement becomes a new issue. Every item is numbered for reference, issues are filed as living, settled or latent, and three manual systems are reported in use with "eager acceptance". It says nothing about what keeping one costs. | Read |
| [NOTE-835](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-835.md) | Grudin — Groupware and social dynamics | An argued review, not a study. Groupware fails less from technical problems than from eight social challenges, first among them that it asks extra work of members who get no direct benefit. The evidence is cases and the literature: meeting schedulers, voice annotation, project management, an abandoned issue-based system. Email succeeds because the sender who does the work is also the one who wants the message read. | Read |
| [NOTE-1446](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1446.md) | Shipman & Marshall — Formality considered harmful | From the authors' experience with hypermedia, design-rationale, knowledge-based, groupware and software-engineering systems: users resist making structure, content or procedure explicit, and are often right to. Formalisms cost cognitive overhead, demand tacit knowledge be stated, commit people to structure too early, and fit only one person, group or task; "there is always information that falls between the cracks". Designers should formalize only what the task needs, infer structure from informal material, and support incremental formalization and restructuring as the task is reconceived. Read in the authors' web version, earlier than the 1999 journal text. | Read |
| [NOTE-1803](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1803.md) | Apostolou, Stojanović, Pariente Lobo, Casas Miró and Papadakis — Configuring E-Government Services Using Ontologies | The paper presents OntoGov (IST-2002-507237), an ontology platform for configuring and reconfiguring e-government services consistently when law or organization changes. | [NOTE-1811](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1811.md) | Herrmannsdoerfer, Benz and Juergens — COPE - Automating Coupled Evolution of Metamodels and Models | When a modeling language's metamodel changes, the existing models must be migrated. The paper calls this pairing "coupled evolution". **The requirements study.** An earlier study of two industrial metamodel histories found: - about half the changes were metamodel-only; - more than three quarters of the coupled changes were metamodel-independent, so they could be reused; - the rest were metamodel-specific; - none were model-specific. This yields two requirements: reuse and expressiveness. **COPE's answer.** A language evolves through a sequence of coupled transactions, each pairing a metamodel adaptation with its model migration. | Read |
| [NOTE-1812](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1812.md) | Song, Cheng, Zhou and Wang — Linking Scholarly Contents: The Design and Construction of an Argumentation Graph | The authors build a knowledge graph of the argumentation inside and across scientific papers. Their data model reuses their earlier Scientific Paper Argumentation Ontology (SAO, built on AMO/Toulmin, DEO, CoreSC, EXPO) with 18 unit classes (background, claim, warrant, backing, rebuttal, conclusion, hypothesis, data, method, limitation, …), 12 intra-article relations (e.g. proves, supports, is part of, is replaced by) and CiTO-based inter-article relations (e.g. works for, provides principles for, provides assertion for). Two tools: an annotation platform (SAPSP) and a d3.js visualizer (VSAG) over Neo4j. | Read |
| [NOTE-1831](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1831.md) | Clark, Ciccarese and Goble — Micropublications: a semantic model for claims, evidence, arguments and annotations in biomedical communications | The paper treats scientific publications as defeasible arguments and proposes "micropublications" as a layered semantic model, available as an OWL vocabulary at purl.org/mp. **Range of the model.** - At its minimum, a micropublication is a statement with its attribution. - At its maximum, it is a Claim with a support graph of Statements, Data and Methods (including Materials), plus a challenge graph. **Relations and constraints.** - Support is transitive. - A challenge is either direct, or indirect by undercutting a supporter. - Within one micropublication, support forms a DAG rooted at the Claim. - A Representation can be asserted by the micropublication or quoted from another one. This is what lets claim networks span publications. **Contrast with statement-based models.** The paper sets micropublications against nanopublications, SWAN and BEL. Those models represent assertions without their evidence, and they cannot close claim lineages down to data. **Examples.** - Example 4 builds claim networks across papers. - Example 5 handles "similogs" (statements with the same meaning) through holotype claims. - Example 8 models challenge and disagreement. **Citation distortion.** The authors apply the model to Greenberg's case of citation distortion, where a claim was upgraded to "fact" through a chain of self-citations. **Implementation.** It is implemented as a plugin to the Domeo annotation tool. | Read |
| [NOTE-1847](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1847.md) | Halilaj, Grangel-González, Coskun and Auer — Git4Voc: Git-based Versioning for Collaborative Vocabulary Development | Collaborative vocabulary development is "the process of finding consensus" among experts from different systems; the authors argue that a version control system is "the heart of the problem" and adapt Git. They list eleven requirements (communication, provenance, roles, workflow independence, quality assurance, documentation, deltas between versions, editor independence, modularity, multilinguality, labeled releases) and meet them with conventions and hooks: issues on GitHub-like platforms for discussion; commit history for provenance; a branching model by kind of change (basic, semantic, structural); server- or client-side hooks that enforce roles and run syntax checks (Rapper) and best-practice checks (OOPS!) before a commit, cancelling it on failure; post-commit documentation generation; one triple per line in Turtle so diffs work; files of at most 300 triples as modules; tags for releases. Git cannot show semantic diffs; external tools are proposed. | Read |
| [NOTE-1848](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1848.md) | Bencomo, Götz and Song — Models@run.time: a guided tour of the state of the art and research challenges | A systematic literature review of 271 papers on models@run.time, mainly since 2006, plus 5 predecessor papers. | [NOTE-1853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1853.md) | Tudorache, Nyulas, Noy and Musen — WebProtégé: A collaborative ontology editor and knowledge acquisition tool for the Web | WebProtégé is a browser-based, lightweight ontology editor built on the Protégé collaborative back end, meant to let domain experts, not only knowledge engineers, edit ontologies. Its interface is a declarative, per-project and per-user configurable portal of portlets and knowledge-acquisition forms bound to ontology properties. Collaboration support includes change tracking (every authoring operation recorded in the Changes and Annotation Ontology, ChAO, with author, time and description), threaded typed notes attached to entities, watches with notifications, change-analysis statistics and a configurable access policy down to property level. | Read |
| [NOTE-1859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1859.md) | Lebo, Sahoo and McGuinness (eds.) — PROV-O: The PROV Ontology | PROV-O is the OWL2 encoding of the PROV Data Model: classes and properties to represent and interchange provenance, i.e. which entities were generated, used, derived, revised, quoted or invalidated by which activities, and which agents were responsible (attribution, association, delegation). Terms come in three tiers: Starting Point (Entity, Activity, Agent, wasGeneratedBy, used, wasDerivedFrom, wasAttributedTo, ...), Expanded (Bundle, Plan, Person, wasRevisionOf, wasQuotedFrom, hadPrimarySource, wasInvalidatedBy, ...) and Qualified terms, which reify a binary influence so further attributes (role, plan, time) can be attached. It is designed to be specialized for domain provenance ontologies. | Skimmed |
